1023.title: Four hundred years of the Granth
1023.hook: Sikhs mark four centuries since the Granth was first installed at the Harmandir
1023.tomorrow: Three hundred years of the Guru Granth
1023.howItsDone: In gurdwaras, the Guru Granth Sahib is carried with honor, placed on a raised seat under a canopy, and opened each morning; Sikhs mark the anniversary of its first installation at the Harmandir Sahib with kirtan and readings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Khalsa's anniversary, and your line was three hundred years. Today the count goes back further, to a book carried into a shrine.

The crowd steps aside for a book. It's wrapped in cloth and carried on someone's head, and behind it walks a man waving a chaur, the whisk of honor, the way you would for a king. At the end of the walk is a shrine standing in a pool, with a raised seat waiting inside. Tradition remembers this as the day the Granth was first set in place at the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar. Centuries later, Sikhs counted back to that day and filled the same walkways. Today: four hundred years of the Granth.
screen: `A BOOK CARRIED ON SOMEONE'S HEAD.` → `A WHISK OF HONOR.` → `FOUR HUNDRED YEARS OF THE GRANTH.`

segments.voice: First, the book. Tradition says Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, gathered the hymns of the Gurus before him, added his own, and included the words of saints from other backgrounds, Hindu and Muslim, whose hymns sang of the One. Bhai Gurdas wrote the volume down as the Guru dictated. Second, the installation. The volume was carried into the Harmandir Sahib and opened there, and tradition says Baba Buddha was appointed to read from it. Third, the seat. The story Sikhs tell is that Guru Arjan had the book placed on a high seat, and sat lower himself. The living Guru sat beneath the book he had compiled: the Word comes first, and even the Guru bows to it. Fourth, the seal. Near the close of the volume comes a short passage known as the Mundavani, at Ang 1429. In it, Guru Arjan says that on this platter three things have been placed: truth, contentment, and contemplation. Anyone who eats from it, he says, is saved. A feast, set out for whoever comes. When Sikhs marked four hundred years, they weren't only honoring an old book. They were remembering the day the platter was first set on the table, and noticing that it's still there, open, every morning.
screen: `GURU ARJAN GATHERS THE HYMNS.` · `CARRIED INTO THE HARMANDIR.` · `THE GURU SITS LOWER.` · `TRUTH, CONTENTMENT, CONTEMPLATION.` · then, large: `FOUR HUNDRED YEARS.`

segments.voice: If you have a gutka, or a page of gurbani on your phone, open it to any page without choosing; if not, picture a book lying open on a cloth. Let your eyes rest on one line, then set three things on an imagined platter in front of you, truth, contentment, contemplation, one breath each, then all three together. If you pray, you can say Waheguru softly between them.
Mundavani. The seal near the close of the Granth, where Guru Arjan says truth, contentment and contemplation are set on the platter for whoever comes. Today's word.
Your line: four hundred years. The Guru sat lower than the Word he gathered. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1023 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THREE HUNDRED YEARS OF THE GURU GRANTH.`

1024.title: Three hundred years of the Guru Granth
1024.hook: Sikhs mark three centuries since the Granth became Guru
1024.tomorrow: Five hundred and fifty years of Nanak
1024.howItsDone: Sikhs bow before the Guru Granth Sahib on entering a gurdwara, read a hukamnama from it each morning, and after the Ardas sangats sing the couplet that commands Sikhs to accept the Granth as Guru.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mundavani, and your line was four hundred years. Today, the same book, a century further on in its story, becomes more than a book.

Each morning in a gurdwara, someone opens the Guru Granth Sahib at random and reads the first hymn on the left-hand page aloud. That reading is the hukamnama, the order of the day. Nobody chooses it; it's received. Sikhs don't treat this as reading a book. They treat it as listening to the Guru. So where did a book get the authority of a living teacher? The answer goes back to a riverbank far to the south of Punjab, at Nanded, and to the last days of the tenth Guru. Today: three hundred years of the Guru Granth.
screen: `OPENED AT RANDOM EACH MORNING.` → `THE ORDER OF THE DAY.` → `A RIVERBANK AT NANDED.`

segments.voice: First, who comes next. For generations, each Guru had named a successor, a living person. Guru Gobind Singh's own sons had all died before him, as this path told in its harder days. Second, the answer at Nanded. Tradition says that there, near the end of his life, Guru Gobind Singh placed the Granth on the seat of the Guru and bowed before it. There would be no human Guru after him. The Word itself would be the Guru, and the Khalsa, the community, would carry on its guidance together. Third, the words people still sing. In gurdwaras, after the Ardas, a couplet from the later tradition is sung. Its sense: by the order of the Timeless One the Panth was founded, and every Sikh is commanded to accept the Granth as Guru. Sikhs name the seat itself gur gaddi, the Guru's throne, and speak of the Guru Granth Sahib as the eternal Guru. Fourth, what it changed. A living Guru can die, be captured, or face rival claimants. A Guru who is the Word is the same wherever it is opened: every gurdwara holds the same Guru, in the same words, on the same raised seat under a canopy. When Sikhs marked three centuries since Nanded, they gathered at Hazur Sahib, the gurdwara there, and in their own gurdwaras, to honor not a person but the Word.
screen: `WHO COMES AFTER THE TENTH GURU?` · `THE GRANTH ON THE GURU'S SEAT.` · `ACCEPT THE GRANTH AS GURU.` · `THE SAME GURU IN EVERY GURDWARA.` · then, large: `THE ETERNAL GURU.`

segments.voice: If you're near the Guru Granth Sahib, you can bow before it, as Sikhs do when they enter; if not, lower your head a little, slowly, toward whatever you hold as wise: a sacred book, a teacher's words, or simply the quiet. Stay low for a few breaths and notice what it feels like to put something above yourself on purpose. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you bow.
Gur gaddi. The Guru's seat, where, tradition says, Guru Gobind Singh placed the Granth at Nanded, and the Word became the eternal Guru. Today's word.
Your line: the eternal guru. No human Guru after the tenth; the Word instead. Day one thousand twenty-four, counted.

screen: `DAY 1024 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: FIVE HUNDRED AND FIFTY YEARS OF NANAK.`

1025.title: Five hundred and fifty years of Nanak
1025.hook: Sikhs and others mark Guru Nanak's birth with celebrations around the world
1025.howItsDone: Sikhs celebrate Guru Nanak's gurpurab with an akhand path ending on the day, nagar kirtan processions, langar and lights; round-number anniversaries are marked with larger gatherings in Punjab and around the world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gur gaddi, and your line was the eternal guru. Today the counting reaches all the way back, to the first Guru's birth.

At dusk, the strings of small lights along a gurdwara roof blink on. Clay lamps line a wall. A procession moves through a city street, the Guru Granth Sahib carried on a decorated float, people sweeping the road clean in front of it, someone handing out sweets at the corner. It looks like a festival of light, and it is one: Guru Nanak's gurpurab, the celebration of his birth. When the count reached a round number, the lights went up in Punjab and far beyond it. Today: five hundred and fifty years of Nanak.
screen: `LIGHTS ON A GURDWARA ROOF.` → `SWEEPING THE ROAD AHEAD.` → `GURU NANAK'S GURPURAB.`

segments.voice: First, the celebration. A gurpurab is a Guru's day. For Guru Nanak's, Sikhs hold an akhand path, an unbroken reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib, ending on the day itself. There are nagar kirtans in the streets, langar for anyone, and lights in the evening. Second, why light. Bhai Gurdas, in his first var, pictures Nanak's coming in a line people still quote: the true Guru Nanak appeared, the mist cleared, and light spread through the world. The lamps on the gurdwara roof are that line, made visible. Third, what scholars notice. The gurpurab is celebrated at the full moon of the month of Kartik, in autumn. Some early accounts of his life place his birth in a different month, in spring, and historians have discussed the difference. Sikh practice keeps the celebration where it is, and both conversations go on side by side. Fourth, the round number. A count like five hundred and fifty is just arithmetic. What makes it matter is what people do with it. When that count came, Sikhs and others marked it with kirtan, langar, lights and service, in villages and in cities across the world. The day wasn't about how long ago Nanak lived. It was about whether his light is still spreading.
screen: `A GURU'S DAY.` · `THE MIST CLEARED, LIGHT SPREAD.` · `KARTIK, OR SPRING?` · `WHAT PEOPLE DO WITH A NUMBER.` · then, large: `FIVE HUNDRED FIFTY YEARS.`

segments.voice: In the procession, people sweep the street before the Guru Granth Sahib passes. Bring to mind one person with a hard road just ahead, an exam, a hospital visit, a new job, a long goodbye, and with each breath out picture clearing one thing from it: a worry, a chore, a stone. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you do.
Gurpurab. A Guru's day: Guru Nanak's birth, marked with akhand path, nagar kirtan, langar and lights around the world. Today's word.
Your line: five hundred fifty years. The mist cleared, and the light spread. That's one thousand twenty-five days.

1026.title: Sikhs in public life abroad
1026.hook: Sikhs now serve in parliaments, courts and city halls in many countries
1026.howItsDone: Sikhs in many countries serve in elected office, the courts, the police and public services, often keeping the turban and articles of faith; every Ardas ends by asking for sarbat da bhala, the good of all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Nanak's gurpurab, and your line was five hundred fifty years. Today, from the Guru's lights to a city hall late at night.

Potholes. That's tonight's business in a half-empty council chamber. A resident at the microphone is complaining about the ones on her street, and she's not wrong. She lives at the far edge of his ward, and she has never voted for the councilor behind the long desk, the one in the navy turban. He takes notes, asks two practical questions, and promises to send someone out on Monday. In parliaments, courtrooms and city halls far from Punjab, scenes like this happen with a turban at the desk. Today: Sikhs in public life abroad.
screen: `A COUNCIL CHAMBER ON A WEEKNIGHT.` → `A TURBAN AT THE DESK.` → `FAR FROM PUNJAB.`

segments.voice: First, the road out. This path has followed Sikhs leaving Punjab: as soldiers, farm workers, students, families starting again. In the countries where they settled, their children and grandchildren grew up as citizens, and some of them stood for office. Today Sikhs serve as lawmakers, judges, mayors, police officers and city staff in a number of countries. Second, the visible faith. Some of them keep the turban and the articles of faith at work. Where a turban was unfamiliar, it became something people saw at the judge's bench and in the debating chamber. Third, the root. In Sorath, at Ang 671 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Arjan says: I have made everyone my friend, and I am a friend to all. And the Ardas, the prayer that closes Sikh gatherings, ends by asking for sarbat da bhala: the good of all. Not the good of Sikhs. The good of all. For a Sikh at a council desk, that's a working brief. Fourth, the test. An elected Sikh speaks for everyone in the district: people of every faith and of none, people who agree and people who never will. The resident at the far edge of the ward, who didn't vote for him, is still his to serve. The pothole on her street is part of the job.
screen: `THE ROAD OUT OF PUNJAB.` · `A TURBAN AT WORK.` · `A FRIEND TO ALL.` · `THE GOOD OF ALL.` · then, large: `SERVING EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Breathe out a wish for the good of the people under your own roof, then widen it with each breath: your street, the neighbors you know and the ones you don't, your town, the people who disagree with you, people across a border you'll never meet. If you pray, you can rest on sarbat da bhala, the good of all, or on Waheguru.
Ardas. The prayer that closes Sikh gatherings, asking for the good of all, the working brief for Sikh lawmakers, judges and mayors serving far from Punjab. Today's word.
Your line: serving everywhere. The good of all reaches the far edge of the ward. Day one thousand twenty-six, done.

1027.title: Explaining the turban
1027.hook: Sikhs around the world invite neighbors to learn about the turban
1027.howItsDone: Sikhs who wear the turban tie it fresh, usually each morning, over uncut hair; some gurdwaras and Sikh student groups hold turban days where neighbors can ask questions and try one on.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ardas, and your line was serving everywhere. Today, a length of cloth people wonder about and rarely ask about.

Why do you wear that every single day? On a college lawn, a student finally asks. There's a folding table, bright lengths of cloth at one end, a mirror at the other, and a hand-lettered sign: ask us anything. A Sikh volunteer smiles and starts winding a long cloth around the student's head, explaining each fold as they go. Minutes later the student is looking in the mirror, a little surprised, still waiting for the answer. Sikhs hold days like this on campuses and in town squares around the world. Today: the answer they give.
screen: `WHY EVERY DAY?` → `A TABLE ON A COLLEGE LAWN.` → `TIE ONE, ASK ANYTHING.`

segments.voice: First, the name. In Punjabi the turban is the dastar, and in everyday speech a pagg. For a Sikh who wears one, it covers the kesh, the uncut hair: the Rehat Maryada, the Sikh code of conduct, asks Sikhs to keep their hair uncut, and the turban keeps it covered. Second, the text. In a hymn of Guru Arjan, at Ang 1084 of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Guru describes, in the words of his Muslim neighbors, what makes a true Muslim, and among its pictures is a form kept whole, with the dastar on the head. The lines around it speak of a heart as soft as wax, and of truth. Sikhs often point to that line when they explain the turban, and notice where it sits: beside inner things, not apart from them. Third, the meaning. Some Sikhs call it a crown, a gift from the Guru. Some speak of a promise worn in public, which makes it harder to break quietly. Tradition says the Gurus wanted a Sikh to be easy to find in a crowd, so that anyone in trouble would know whom to ask for help. Some Sikh women wear a turban too; others cover their hair with a long scarf, a chunni. Fourth, the invitation. Sikhs have been taken for people they are not, and sometimes harassed for it. So some gurdwaras and student groups answer with an open table instead of a complaint. Their bet is simple: a neighbor who has asked one real question, and heard one real answer, looks at a turban differently afterward.

Say it to yourself on the breath in and let it settle on the breath out; if you pray, you can say Waheguru instead.

1028.title: Langar on the highway
1028.hook: in the farmers' protests of 2020 and 2021 langar fed protesters on the roads
1028.howItsDone: Sikhs serve langar, a free communal meal, at gurdwaras, and volunteers often take it out to where people gather, at protests, disasters and long journeys.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dastar, and your line was ask, then learn. Today, a kitchen that refused to stay indoors.

Tractors parked nose to tail along a highway, as far down the road as the eye can follow. Behind them, steam rising from huge pots. Somebody kneading dough on a tarp. Somebody flipping rotis on a wide iron griddle. A row of people sitting on the asphalt, plates in their laps. Farmers had come to the edges of Delhi to protest new farm laws, and they camped there, on the roads, through heat and through cold. A camp that size needs feeding. Nobody set up a canteen with a cash register. They set up langar.
screen: `TRACTORS ALONG THE HIGHWAY.` → `POTS, DOUGH, A GRIDDLE.` → `NOT A CANTEEN. LANGAR.`

segments.voice: First, the camp. People held different views about the farm laws, and this lesson isn't here to settle that. It's here for the kitchen. Among the farmers on the roads were Sikhs from Punjab, and they brought what Sikhs bring when a crowd gathers: rations, cooks, and the habit of feeding anyone who sits down. Second, the root. Langar is the free kitchen of the Guru's house, and Sikh tradition traces it back to the Gurus themselves. In a hymn by the bards Satta and Balwand, at Ang 967 of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Guru's langar runs on, and its stores never run short. The same hymn praises Mata Khivi, the wife of Guru Angad, who served in the langar, giving out rich rice pudding made with ghee, and whose kindness gave wide shade. From the start, langar was a kitchen with names and hands. Third, the road. On the highway, langar did what it does in a gurdwara: it didn't check who you were. Farmers ate, and so did passersby, reporters, and people who simply lived nearby and walked over. Volunteers washed dishes on the roadside; some kept pots going through the night. Fourth, the point. A gurdwara is a building, but langar was never really about the building. It's a habit: where people gather, cook; where people are tired, feed them; and sit together, in a row, on the same ground. When the farmers moved onto the road, the kitchen didn't wait for them to come back.
screen: `DIFFERENT VIEWS. TODAY, THE KITCHEN.` · `ANG 967: STORES THAT NEVER RUN SHORT.` · `FARMERS, PASSERSBY, NEIGHBORS.` · `NOT THE BUILDING. THE HABIT.` · then, large: `THE KITCHEN CAME ALONG.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who is worn out right now, a parent on night shifts, a friend in a hard month, a coworker carrying too much, and see their face. On a breath out, ask one plain question, what could I bring them to eat or drink, and let one answer arrive without planning the whole thing. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
Langar. The Guru's free kitchen, which went with farmers camped on the highway and fed whoever sat down. Today's word.
Your line: the kitchen came along. Langar goes where the people are. Day one thousand twenty-eight, done.

1029.title: Afghanistan's Sikhs
1029.hook: an old Sikh community in Afghanistan shrank to a handful after attacks, and many left
1029.howItsDone: Afghan Sikh families who settled in India, Britain, Canada and elsewhere keep their own gurdwaras and remember those killed in the attacks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, langar, and your line was the kitchen came along. Today, a community that had to carry its whole life along.

Sikh families once lived and traded in Afghanistan's cities, spoke the local languages, and kept their gurdwaras behind plain doorways in the old lanes of Kabul. Step through one of those doorways: a hall with a canopy, a covered Guru Granth Sahib, a few families on the floor, a harmonium, a kitchen in the back. Then came the attacks. A gurdwara in Kabul was struck during prayers, and worshipers were killed. After that, family after family packed what they could and left. Today is about the ones who left, and the few who stayed.
screen: `A DOORWAY IN OLD KABUL.` → `A HALL, A CANOPY, A KITCHEN.` → `THEN THE ATTACKS.`

segments.voice: First, the roots. Tradition says Guru Nanak's travels reached the lands to the west, and Afghan Sikhs have long told that story as part of their own. They speak of families who lived there for generations, alongside Hindu neighbors, as shopkeepers, traders and healers who sold herbal remedies, and the gurdwara was where the community gathered. Second, the attacks. There was more than one. A bombing in Jalalabad killed Sikh and Hindu community leaders on their way to meet the president. Later, gunmen attacked a gurdwara in Kabul during morning prayers. A place built for gathering became the place that was hardest to gather in. Third, the leaving. Families left for India, and from there some went on to other countries. Reports tell of saroops, copies of the Guru Granth Sahib, carried out with great care, wrapped and held high, as people do when they move the Guru. Leaving a country is hard. Leaving it while carrying the Guru is a different kind of journey. Fourth, the text. In a hymn of Guru Nanak, at Ang 72 of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Guru asks how the true sangat is known, and answers: it is where the one Name is praised. He gives no number. A few families still gathering around the Guru in a back lane are, in that line, a sangat. Size doesn't decide belonging.
screen: `OLD ROOTS IN KABUL.` · `A GURDWARA ATTACKED AT PRAYER.` · `CARRYING THE GURU OUT.` · `ANG 72: WHERE THE NAME IS PRAISED.` · then, large: `A SMALL COMMUNITY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a gathering that has grown smaller than it used to be: Afghanistan's Sikhs, if you like, or a congregation, a club, a family table with empty chairs. Picture the few who still turn up, and with each breath out, wish them steadiness. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer or say Waheguru; if you don't, simply keep them in mind.
Afghanistan's Sikhs. An old community that, after attacks, shrank to a handful, while many families left carrying the Guru with them. Today's word.
Your line: a small community. Small in number, and not small in the eyes of the Guru. That's day one thousand twenty-nine.
